items.question: Why does the method in paper3 rely on global recomputation after small graph changes instead of updating the learned model with new short random walks from the changed region?

items.correction: The method updates the learned model with new random walks from the changed region in time sub-linear to the entire graph, without global recomputation.
items.evidence_quote: We can iteratively update the learned model with new random walks from the changed region in time sub-linear to the entire graph.

items.question: Under which conditions does the model in paper3 need the Wikipedia article corpus to train its graph embeddings, given that it models English text frequencies directly from the network?

items.correction: The paper uses the text of 100,000 articles from the English Wikipedia only as an example of a similar power-law distribution; it is not training graph embeddings on English text frequency data.
items.evidence_quote: The first comes from a series of short random walks on a scale-free graph, and the second comes from the text of 100,000 articles from the English Wikipedia.

items.question: What comparison result does paper3 report between random-walk frequencies and word frequencies in natural language, and why does the method conclude they are unrelated distributions?
items.false_premise: The paper reports that random-walk frequencies and word frequencies are unrelated distributions.

items.evidence_quote: Word frequency in natural language follows a similar distribution, and techniques from language modeling account for this distributional behavior.
